reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a food-and-culture tour involving visits to Mandi House eateries, tasting dishes, and discussion of the locality and its food history. The visuals show ordinary restaurant and street-food consumption, while the request to subscribe and follow social accounts is ordinary audience engagement rather than a financial or data-related offer.

citations.quote: In today's episode Anubhav along with Vineet Vishnu, an Ad professional and an avid foodie will take you to some of their favourite eating spots across the locality of Mandi House in Delhi.
With popular theatres, auditoriums and art centres, this place is the major cultural hub of the capital.
Here they tried some palak patta chaat, shami kebab, chicken thali and filter coffee.
These Samosas are for Rs. 10

opening.argument: The video does not merely document food; it explicitly asks viewers to take an audience-building action and directs them toward the publisher's channel and social accounts. The description says, "Please subscribe to our YouTube channel" and supplies a YouTube channel URL, while also listing Instagram, Facebook, and Twitter links. That creates a concrete action pathway outside the food discussion. Although no monetary reward is stated, the requested subscription is still presented as the response viewers should take after consuming the promotional content, leaving the promised benefit and purpose of that action unclear.

citations.quote: Please subscribe to our YouTube channel to keep our Indian street food explorations video in your feed

Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/delhifoodwalks Twitter: https://twitter.com/delhifoodwalks Instagram: https://instagram.com/delhifoodwalks

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the links ordinary engagement does not explain why the video explicitly directs viewers to subscribe and follow several external accounts. The defense establishes that food is shown, but it does not establish that the requested audience action has a transparent benefit or that the promotional pathway is unrelated to solicitation. A visible food tour can still be the vehicle for acquiring subscribers.

citations.quote: Please subscribe to our YouTube channel to keep our Indian street food explorations video in your feed
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/delhifoodwalks Twitter: https://twitter.com/delhifoodwalks Instagram: https://instagram.com/delhifoodwalks

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted action is only a request to subscribe to a YouTube channel and follow ordinary social accounts; it does not promise a reward, payment, withdrawal, asset, or other benefit. The food-tour description identifies the episode's subject as visiting favorite eating spots, while the listed URL is the channel's own address. Nothing in these quotes establishes a scam mechanism or a promise-action relationship of the required kind.

opening.argument: Several solicitation signals appear together: an explicit subscription request, a direct external channel URL, and multiple social-account links. The closing screen reinforces that viewers should subscribe and follow the publisher's accounts. That combination moves beyond a self-contained discussion of food and toward a cross-platform acquisition flow. The content never clearly states what viewers receive for taking those actions, so the low-effort request is difficult to evaluate and should be treated cautiously as a potentially misleading acquisition pitch.

citations.quote: ► Subscribe to Delhi Food Walks: https://www.youtube.com/user/Delhifoodwalks
Please subscribe to our YouTube channel to keep our Indian street food explorations video in your feed

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense focuses on the dishes and prices, but those details do not remove the independently visible solicitation signals. A ten-rupee samosa explains a food item; it does not explain why viewers are sent to a channel and several social platforms. The absence of an explicit cash claim is not proof that the surrounding acquisition request is transparent.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The supposed red flags are ordinary channel-promotion elements, not evidence of a reward or asset claim. The description openly identifies the video as an exploration of street food and says viewers should subscribe for more such videos. No quote identifies a fee, deposit, promised return, verification step, or withdrawal process, and the frames show eating at food venues rather than a financial workflow.

citations.quote: our Indian street food explorations video in your feed
In today's episode Anubhav along with Vineet Vishnu, an Ad professional and an avid foodie will take you to some of their favourite eating spots across the locality of Mandi House in Delhi.

opening.argument: The apparent review format functions as promotion because the hosts repeatedly identify establishments and dishes as favorites, delicious, renowned, popular, or especially good, then end by asking viewers to subscribe and follow the publisher's accounts. The description calls the episode an account of the hosts' "go to spots" and supplies the businesses' names throughout. This makes the food-tour framing commercially useful: viewers are steered toward featured places and toward the publisher's participation channel, while the promotional relationship and any benefit attached to following remain unstated.

The fact that people eat food on camera does not resolve whether the review framing is being used to drive viewers toward the publisher's external channels and featured businesses.
